children: By Dan Levine and Jonathan Stempel
PacifiCorp utility said on Saturday it welcomed a decision by the Oregon Supreme Court to look into all potential errors in the handling of a wildfire class-action against the company.

Oregon residents and business owners who want PacifiCorp to be held liable for four wildfires in 2020 hope to reverse a state appeals court's decision that wiped out $1.25 billion of awards to 201 plaintiffs because of an error with the instructions to jurors.

But the state's highest court on Friday expanded its review of the case to include all possible errors raised in the appeal, not just the jury instructions. That may increase the possibility that the state Supreme Court will find problems in the trial judge's handling of the litigation, including whether he should have certified a class to begin with.
Friday's decision means Portland-based PacifiCorp will not face additional so-called mini-trials over its liability to fire victims while the appeals process continues.

“The Court recognizes the litany of missteps in this case, and we remain confident that sound legal principles and facts will prevail," Ryan Flynn, president of PacifiCorp's Pacific Power division, said in a statement released on Saturday.
Attorneys for the plaintiffs did not immediately comment on the order.
If plaintiffs win the lawsuit, PacifiCorp could face tens of billions of dollars in potential damages over its role in the 2020 wildfires.

More than 2,400 plaintiffs blamed the Portland-based utility's equipment and alleged negligent failure to shut down power lines during a Labor Day weekend windstorm for damaging more than 2,000 properties. The state's high court heard oral arguments in the case earlier this month.
The appeals court's decision focused on the jury instruction by Multnomah County Circuit Court Judge Steffan Alexander, and not whether a class action was justified.
Friday's order set deadlines in early 2027 for the parties to file briefs on the broader set of appellate issues.
